theme: The LORD reigns; holy is he
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 99. This is the last of a short series of psalms that proclaim “the LORD reigns.” Read it for its repeated refrain, “Holy is he,” and notice how Moses, Aaron, and Samuel appear.
settingTheScene: Psalm 99 is a psalm of praise to the LORD as king. It has three sections, each ending with a refrain about God’s holiness. Unlike the more joyful psalms, this one stresses awe and reverence. It appears here because the story of Numbers has shown what happens when people forget that the God who lives among them is holy. It also mentions Moses and Aaron, the leaders of the wilderness generation.
observation: “The LORD reigns; let the peoples tremble! He sits enthroned upon the cherubim; let the earth quake!” (v. 1).
“The LORD is great in Zion; he is exalted over all the peoples” (v. 2).
“Let them praise your great and awesome name! Holy is he!” (v. 3).
“The King in his might loves justice. You have established equity; you have executed justice and righteousness in Jacob” (v. 4).
“Exalt the LORD our God; worship at his footstool! Holy is he!” (v. 5).
“Moses and Aaron were among his priests, Samuel also was among those who called upon his name” (v. 6).
“You were a forgiving God to them, but an avenger of their wrongdoings” (v. 8).
“Exalt the LORD our God, and worship at his holy mountain; for the LORD our God is holy!” (v. 9).
interpretation:
The refrain, “Holy is he,” gives the psalm its shape. The first section celebrates God’s rule over the nations, the second his love of justice, and the third his dealings with his people in history. Each ends with the same note. Holiness is not one attribute among many. It is the character that sets God apart from everything else, the quality that makes his power safe and his justice trustworthy.

It is notable that holiness and justice go together here. The “King in his might loves justice.” A holy God is not just distant and awesome. He cares about equity. His holiness shows itself in how he rules, which is fairly and truly.

The third section is the most important for this unit. It remembers Moses, Aaron, and Samuel, who called on the LORD, and says that he answered them. He spoke to them in the pillar of cloud. This is a reference to the wilderness generation. The psalm then says something that holds together the whole book of Numbers: “You were a forgiving God to them, but an avenger of their wrongdoings.” Both are true. God forgave Israel at Kadesh, and God also let a generation die in the wilderness. He is merciful, and he is holy. Neither cancels the other.

This is a difficult balance to keep. We tend to emphasize one side and neglect the other. The psalm holds both. It encourages us to approach God as forgiving and to remember that he is holy. This is exactly what Moses prayed in Exodus 34. The same pairing appears in the apostles: grace and truth, kindness and severity.

After a week of reading about people who tested God, it is good to end with a psalm that tells us to worship him at his footstool.
connection: In Isaiah 6, the seraphim cry, “Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts,” and John says that Isaiah saw Christ’s glory (John 12:41). Revelation 4:8 repeats the cry before the throne. Paul says, “Note then the kindness and the severity of God” (Romans 11:22). Peter writes, “You shall be holy, for I am holy” (1 Peter 1:16). Hebrews 12:28-29 calls us to worship with reverence and awe.
application:
Read the psalm aloud, and pause at each “Holy is he.” Think about what holiness means to you.

Ask whether you have emphasized God’s mercy at the expense of his holiness, or the other way around.

Thank God for his forgiveness, and ask him to make you holy.
prayerPrompts: Worship the LORD as holy, in your own words.
Thank him that he forgives and is also just.
Ask him to teach you reverence and awe.
